assumptions: A formally consented family-company pilot can be conducted without privileged access or implicit customer rights.
One narrow workflow can be standardized across a meaningful share of field-service SMEs.
Human approval remains in place for financially or operationally consequential actions.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Paid pilots showing baseline-to-post-deployment labor savings, acceptable error rates, low monthly exception hours, strong gross contribution, renewal intent, and repeatable acquisition beyond the family relationship.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: A vertical, human-in-loop service can bridge the gap between capable AI tools and SMEs unable to deploy reliable cross-application workflows.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Administrative labor, backlog, and errors are tangible costs, but hours saved, acceptable error rates, and Polish owner willingness to pay are not measured.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Setup fees and prepaid retainers offer good cash conversion, yet customization, monitoring, and exception labor could undermine the assumed margins and scale.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Renewable installers or another field-service vertical is narrow, reachable, and replicable across many SMEs, though the initial workflow definition needs further narrowing.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Vertical templates and operational knowledge could establish a niche, but local implementers and rapidly improving horizontal suites limit domination potential.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A proven workflow can extend across functions, adjacent field-service verticals, and CEE markets with shared process patterns.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Exception data, templates, and embedded workflows can accumulate, but integrations are nonexclusive and platform vendors may absorb common functions.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Outcome-focused implementation and ongoing exception handling are more useful than generic AI access, but no demonstrated savings or reliability advantage exists.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Improving AI capability and low Polish adoption create a service-to-software window, although low adoption may reflect weak demand or readiness.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: A lawful family-company pilot and accountant or reseller referrals offer practical entry, but scalable channel commitments and acquisition economics are absent.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The founder's skills, modest capital need, and measurable pilot design fit well, while security, integration fragility, and service creep remain manageable but significant.

highest_value_structural_change: Narrow the offer to one high-frequency workflow in one field-service vertical and price against independently measured labor savings with a standardized integration stack.
main_structural_strength: The founder can cheaply validate a recurring, AI-leveraged service in an accessible vertical before committing substantial capital.
primary_score_limiter: Unproven standardization and support intensity leave open the risk that this becomes a custom automation agency rather than scalable equity.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Poland's unusually low AI adoption may reflect limited willingness or capability to buy, while horizontal software vendors are rapidly commoditizing administrative automation.
